RULES|8|Order of instructions|A police officer signals you to stop while your traffic light is green. What should you do?|Stop as directed by the officer.|A police officer's directions take precedence over traffic signals, signs and general rules.|Follow the green light~The officer's instruction has higher priority than the light.|Stop only if there is a stop sign~The police instruction is sufficient.|Continue if the road looks clear~A clear road does not cancel the instruction.

RULES|23|Giving way|You approach a give-way sign with a clear view and no conflicting traffic. What is required?|Slow down, check carefully and stop only if necessary.|Giving way requires you to avoid obstructing intersecting traffic; a complete stop is not automatic.|Always stop for five seconds~A give-way sign does not impose a fixed stop.|Maintain speed because the road is empty~You must clearly demonstrate readiness to yield.|Give way only to vehicles from the right~The duty covers traffic from both directions.

RULES|24|Stop line|You reach a stop sign with a marked stop line and no other traffic. Where must you stop?|Immediately before the stop line.|A stop sign requires a complete stop even when the road appears empty.|Beside the sign regardless of the line~The marked stop line determines the stopping point.|Only after entering the junction~That puts the car into conflicting traffic.|There is no need to stop~The stop obligation is unconditional.

RULES|24|Queue at a stop sign|The car ahead stops at a stop line. You stop behind it. What must you do when you reach the line?|Make your own complete stop at the line.|Each driver must fulfil the stop obligation at the proper stopping point.|Follow without stopping again~The other driver's stop does not fulfil your obligation.|Stop only if someone approaches~The obligation applies even without traffic.|Sound the horn before proceeding~A horn is not a substitute for stopping.

RULES|26|Priority to the right|Two vehicles meet at an unsigned junction where no other priority rule applies. Who must you give way to?|Vehicles approaching from your right.|The priority-to-the-right rule applies when no sign, signal or other priority rule replaces it.|Vehicles from the left only~This reverses the rule.|Only larger vehicles~Vehicle size does not establish priority.|Nobody if your road is wider~Road width alone does not change the rule.

RULES|28|Different road widths|A car approaches from your right on a narrower normal road at an otherwise unsigned junction. What applies?|You give way to it.|A wider road is not automatically a priority road.|The narrower road always gives way~Width alone is not a priority rule.|You go first if travelling straight~Going straight does not override priority to the right.|The faster car goes first~Speed never creates priority.

RULES|30|Open parking areas|Two moving cars cross paths inside an open car park, away from parking spaces. No signs regulate priority. What normally applies?|Give way to the vehicle on your right.|Priority to the right can apply in open areas as well as conventional junctions.|All traffic gives way to the left~That is not the general rule.|Only painted junctions have priority rules~Markings are not necessary for the rule.|The first car to sound its horn goes first~A horn cannot establish priority.

RULES|35|Leaving a property|You drive from a house driveway onto a road. What is your obligation?|Give way to road users whose paths you cross.|Leaving a property is covered by the exit rule.|Give way only to the right~The exit rule is broader than priority to the right.|Join first if turning right~The turn does not remove the exit obligation.|Claim priority because you started moving~Starting first does not establish priority.

RULES|35|Crossing an uninterrupted cycle path|You leave a property across an uninterrupted cycle path before joining the road. What must you do?|Give way on both the cycle path and the road.|The exit rule applies to the path you cross and the road you enter.|Give way only on the road~Cyclists on the uninterrupted path also have protection.|Cyclists must always stop for cars~Cars do not have general priority over cyclists.|Treat the cycle path as a parking strip~It is a route for cyclists, not parking.

RULES|33|Turning left|You have a round green light and want to turn left across an oncoming car's path. What applies?|Let the oncoming car pass before turning.|A round green light may also be shown to oncoming traffic; turning duties still apply.|Green gives you priority in every direction~Green does not cancel the turning rule.|Turn immediately because you indicated~An indicator communicates intention, not priority.|The oncoming car must stop for a left turn~It is your turn that crosses its path.

RULES|38|Blocked junction|Your signal turns green, but the road beyond the junction is blocked. What should you do?|Wait before entering until you can clear the junction.|You must avoid becoming stationary where you obstruct crossing traffic.|Enter because the signal is green~Green does not authorise blocking the junction.|Stop in the middle to reserve your place~That obstructs other traffic.|Drive onto the pedestrian crossing and wait~The crossing must also be kept clear.

RULES|39|Bus leaving a stop|On a road limited to 50 km/h, a bus signals to leave a stop into your lane, the rightmost lane. What must you do?|Slow down and let the bus leave.|At a speed limit of 50 km/h or lower, drivers in the affected lane must allow a signalling bus out.|Accelerate past before it moves~That frustrates the bus rule.|The bus always has to wait~The 50 km/h rule applies here.|Stop in the opposing lane~That introduces a new danger.

RULES|39|Bus on a faster road|The speed limit is 70 km/h and a bus signals to leave its stop. Which statement is correct?|The bus must give way, but you should still be ready to cooperate.|The special obligation to let a bus out applies at limits of 50 km/h or lower.|The bus always has unconditional priority~The limit is above the bus-rule threshold.|You should block the bus deliberately~All drivers still owe care and consideration.|The bus may pull out without looking~Its driver must avoid danger.

RULES|40|Amber light|A light changes from green to amber and you can stop safely before the line. What must you do?|Stop before the line.|Amber means stop unless you are so close that stopping safely is no longer possible.|Accelerate to beat red~Amber is not an invitation to speed up.|Continue whenever the junction is empty~An empty junction does not remove the stop requirement.|Wait until red before braking~That can make the stop unsafe or too late.

RULES|40|Flashing amber|Traffic signals are flashing amber. How do you determine priority?|Use the applicable signs or general priority rules with extra caution.|Flashing amber warns that normal signal control is not operating.|Treat it as a permanent green light~It grants no general right to proceed.|Treat every approach as a priority road~Priority must come from signs or rules.|Ignore pedestrians until signals recover~Pedestrian duties still apply.

RULES|41|Red and amber together|Your traffic signal displays red and amber together. What does it mean?|Remain stopped; green is about to appear.|The combined signal still requires you to stop.|Start moving across the line~The signal has not yet permitted movement.|Proceed if turning right~There is no general right turn on red.|Only pedestrians must wait~The signal applies to the drivers facing it.

RULES|46|Uncontrolled pedestrian crossing|A pedestrian is about to enter an uncontrolled crossing. What should you do?|Clearly slow down and give way.|Drivers must give way to pedestrians on or about to enter an uncontrolled crossing.|Continue until the pedestrian steps into your lane~The duty begins before they reach your lane.|Sound the horn to make them wait~A horn does not replace giving way.|Give way only to children~The crossing rule protects all pedestrians.

RULES|46|Walking a bicycle|A person pushes a bicycle over a pedestrian crossing. How are they treated?|As a pedestrian.|A person walking with a bicycle is a pedestrian rather than a riding cyclist.|As a motor vehicle~A pushed bicycle is not a motor vehicle.|As a cyclist who is riding~They are walking rather than riding.|As someone prohibited from crossing~Pushing a bicycle is allowed.

RULES|50|Bicycle passage on a straight road|You drive straight towards an uncontrolled bicycle passage. Which duty applies to you?|Adapt speed so you do not endanger cyclists already on the passage.|The cyclist's obligation to give way does not remove the driver's duty to avoid danger.|Maintain speed regardless of cyclists~Drivers still have a safety obligation.|Treat it as an automatic green signal~No signal is present.|Accelerate to force cyclists to stop~Deliberately creating danger is unacceptable.

RULES|50|Bicycle passage after a turn|You turn across an uncontrolled bicycle passage. A cyclist is about to enter it. What should you do?|Drive slowly and give the cyclist an opportunity to pass.|Turning drivers and drivers exiting a roundabout have additional duties at bicycle passages.|Use your indicator to force the cyclist to wait~Indicating does not remove the obligation.|Apply only the straight-road situation~The turning situation has additional duties.|Stop on the passage to block it~That obstructs the cyclist's route.

RULES|52|Bicycle crossing|A signed bicycle crossing has the prescribed markings. A cyclist is about to use it. What applies?|You must give way to the cyclist.|A bicycle crossing has an explicit driver duty to yield to cyclists using or about to use it.|Cyclists always yield because they are smaller~Vehicle size does not establish priority.|The rule applies only to pedestrians~This is a bicycle crossing.|The cyclist must dismount first~Dismounting is not required at a bicycle crossing.

RULES|58|Entering a roundabout|You approach a signed roundabout. Who must you give way to?|All vehicles already circulating in it.|The entry obligation applies to circulating vehicles, including bicycles.|Only vehicles from your right~Roundabout entry has its own rule.|Only motor vehicles~Bicycles are vehicles too.|Nobody if you are taking the first exit~Your intended exit does not remove the duty.

RULES|58|Leaving a roundabout|Which signal is required when leaving a roundabout?|Indicate right.|An exit is a movement to the right and must be signalled.|Indicate left until fully outside~That gives the wrong exit message.|Use hazard warning lights~Hazard lights do not indicate a normal exit.|No signal if travelling straight overall~You still need to signal the exit.

RULES|58|Changing roundabout lanes|You are in an inner roundabout lane and want to cross the outer lane to exit. What must you do?|Check and change lanes only without danger or obstruction.|Being in the inner lane does not give priority over traffic in the outer lane.|Force outer-lane traffic to stop~Lane changes must be safe.|Exit immediately whenever you indicate~Indicating does not create a gap.|Stop abruptly in the circulating lane~An abrupt stop can cause a collision; continue around if needed.

RULES|68|Stopping in a tunnel|May you make a voluntary stop in a road tunnel to check directions?|No; continue to a suitable permitted stopping place.|Voluntary stopping and parking in a tunnel are prohibited.|Yes with hazard lights~Hazard lights do not legalise a voluntary stop.|Yes for less than one minute~Duration does not create an exception.|Yes if the engine stays on~Engine status does not change the restriction.

RULES|69|Before a pedestrian crossing|You want to park 6 metres before a pedestrian crossing. Is this permitted?|No, stopping and parking are prohibited within 10 metres before it.|A vehicle there can hide pedestrians from approaching drivers.|Yes if you remain in the car~Remaining inside does not remove the prohibition.|Yes if the crossing is empty~The distance rule still applies.|Yes if the car is small~Vehicle size does not remove the rule.

RULES|70|Waiting for a passenger|You wait at the roadside for a friend who is still inside a building. What is this normally classed as?|Parking.|Waiting is parking when no actual boarding, alighting, loading or unloading is taking place.|Always loading~Waiting for a person is not loading goods.|Never parking if the engine runs~A running engine does not change the definition.|A traffic-required stop~The traffic situation did not require you to wait.

RULES|71|Priority-road parking|May you park on a priority road where there is no sign permitting parking?|No.|Parking on a priority road is generally prohibited unless parking is specifically permitted.|Yes whenever there is a hard shoulder~A shoulder alone is not permission.|Yes for 24 hours~The ordinary parking time rule does not override this prohibition.|Yes with parking lights~Lights improve visibility but do not create permission.

RULES|71|Level-crossing parking|You want to park 20 metres from a railway crossing. What applies?|Parking is prohibited within 30 metres of the crossing.|The parking restriction extends 30 metres on either side of a railway or tramway crossing.|Parking is prohibited only on the rails~The restriction extends beyond the rails.|Parking is allowed if no train is visible~Train visibility does not change the distance rule.|Only large vehicles are prohibited~The restriction also applies to cars.

RULES|72|One-way parking|On which side may you park on a one-way street, if signs and other rules permit?|Either side.|One-way streets are an exception to the usual right-side stopping and parking rule.|Only on the right in all cases~One-way streets allow the left side too.|Only in the middle~Parking in the middle would obstruct traffic.|On the pavement~One-way status does not permit pavement parking.

RULES|73|Date parking|Date parking applies today, an even-numbered date. Which side is prohibited?|The side with even house numbers.|During the restriction's hours, the date and prohibited side have the same parity.|The side with odd numbers~That reverses the date-parking rule.|Both sides all day~Check the sign's times; the rule identifies one side.|Neither side on even dates~Even dates are covered by the rule.

RULES|73|Parking time panels|What do times in parentheses on a parking panel normally refer to?|Weekdays before Sundays and public holidays.|Parentheses cover the day before a Sunday or public holiday, not just ordinary Saturdays.|Only Sundays~Sundays and public holidays normally use red times.|Every weekday~Ordinary weekday times are shown without parentheses.|Only school holidays~School holidays do not define these times.

RULES|74|Bus-stop space|At an unmarked bus stop, where does the stopping restriction normally extend?|20 metres before and 5 metres after the stop sign.|The larger approach space allows a bus to enter its stop.|5 metres before and 20 after~That reverses the distances.|Exactly 10 metres on both sides~Those are not the bus-stop distances.|Only directly beside the sign~The protected area extends beyond the sign.

RULES|74|Picking up at a bus stop|May you briefly pick up a passenger at a bus stop?|Only if you do not hinder bus or tram traffic.|Actual boarding and alighting may be allowed, but the stop must remain usable by public transport.|Yes even if a bus must wait~You must not hinder the bus.|Only if you are also unloading furniture~Goods unloading is not the passenger exception.|Never under any circumstances~A limited passenger exception exists.

RULES|91|Motorway exit missed|You miss your motorway exit. What should you do?|Continue to the next suitable exit.|Reversing or turning around on a motorway is prohibited.|Reverse along the shoulder~Reversing is prohibited even on the shoulder.|Use an opening in the central barrier~Such openings are not for ordinary U-turns.|Stop and walk back to the exit~Stopping and walking on the motorway are not permitted for this purpose.

RULES|91|Acceleration lane|You join a motorway using an acceleration lane. What approach is correct?|Adapt your speed and cooperate with traffic to merge safely.|Both entering and existing traffic must show consideration and adapt.|Entering traffic has absolute priority~The lane does not grant absolute priority.|Motorway traffic must always stop~Stopping is not the normal merging method.|Merge without checking the blind spot~Mirrors alone can miss nearby vehicles.

RULES|91|Motorway eligibility|May a class I moped use a motorway because it can travel at 45 km/h?|No, mopeds are prohibited.|The design-speed requirement does not override the specific ban on mopeds.|Yes because 45 is above 40~Mopeds are explicitly excluded.|Yes on the shoulder only~The shoulder is not a moped route.|Yes if the driver holds a B licence~The vehicle prohibition still applies.

RULES|99|Overtaking at a crossing|On a normal two-way road, may you overtake a car immediately before an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing?|No.|Overtaking there can hide pedestrians and is prohibited.|Yes if you sound the horn~A horn does not create an exception.|Yes if the car is slow~Its speed does not remove the prohibition.|Yes if the centre line is broken~A broken line does not override the crossing restriction.

RULES|101|Overtaking speed|May you exceed the posted speed limit briefly to finish overtaking?|No.|The speed limit still applies during an overtake.|Yes by up to 10 km/h~There is no general overtaking allowance.|Yes for less than five seconds~Duration does not legalise speeding.|Yes if the other driver agrees~Another driver's agreement cannot change the limit.

RULES|108|Railway priority|A train approaches, but the railway crossing's red lights are not flashing. What must you do?|Give way to the train.|You must check for trains and yield even if warning equipment is not operating.|Cross because the red light is off~The absence of a red signal is not a guarantee.|Sound your horn and cross~A train cannot readily stop or swerve.|Expect the train to give way~Road vehicles yield to trains.

RULES|110|Queue beyond the railway|The traffic beyond a railway crossing has stopped, leaving no room for your car. What should you do?|Wait before the crossing until your whole vehicle can clear it.|Never enter a crossing if you risk stopping on the tracks.|Enter while the barriers are open~Open barriers do not make the space beyond sufficient.|Stop with only the rear over the rails~Any part of the car on the track is dangerous.|Follow closely to claim the gap~That can trap your car on the crossing.

RULES|116|Home-zone speed|A signed home zone appears empty. How fast may you drive?|At walking speed.|The walking-speed rule applies even when no pedestrian is visible.|At 30 km/h~A home zone is not an ordinary 30 zone.|At 50 km/h~The home-zone rule replaces the ordinary limit.|As fast as visibility allows~Walking speed remains the maximum.

RULES|117|Bicycle-street speed|You drive on a signed bicycle street. What speed rule applies?|Adapt to cyclists and never exceed 30 km/h.|The maximum is 30 km/h, but cyclists may require a lower speed.|Always drive exactly 30 km/h~Adaptation may require a much lower speed.|Walking speed in every case~That is the home-zone rule, not the bicycle-street maximum.|50 km/h when cyclists are absent~The 30 km/h maximum still applies.

RULES|117|Pedestrian-street access|May you use a pedestrian street as a convenient through route in your car?|No, ordinary through driving is not an authorised purpose.|Only specified essential access is allowed, such as certain deliveries or access to homes.|Yes if you drive at walking speed~Speed compliance alone does not authorise access.|Yes if there are no pedestrians~Absence of pedestrians does not permit through driving.|Yes after dark~The access restriction does not disappear at night.

RULES|262|Dipped and fog lights|May you use dipped headlights and front fog lights together?|No.|This combination is prohibited; use the permitted lighting appropriate to visibility.|Yes in all darkness~Darkness does not permit that combination.|Yes if your car is new~Vehicle age does not change the rule.|Yes when overtaking~Overtaking creates no lighting exception.

RULES|263|Signalling on a priority road|A priority road bends right at a junction and you follow it. Must you indicate the turn?|Yes, signal your change of direction.|Priority does not replace communicating your intention to turn.|No because you remain on the priority road~The direction change still needs signalling.|Only if leaving the priority road~It is the manoeuvre that matters.|Use the left indicator~That communicates the opposite direction.

PERSONAL|132|Deep learning|Which way of studying driving theory is most likely to build lasting understanding?|Understanding why rules exist and applying them to new situations.|Deep learning connects rules to their purpose, helping you handle unfamiliar situations.|Memorising only the answer letters~Letters can change and do not teach the rule.|Skipping explanations after correct answers~You may miss the reasoning needed in a different situation.|Learning only the easiest questions~That leaves important gaps in knowledge.

PERSONAL|132|Overlearning|Why should basic vehicle controls become well practised?|So more attention is available for traffic and hazards.|When gear changing and other controls become familiar, they require less conscious effort.|So you can stop observing the road~Observation remains essential.|So the car will never skid~Practice cannot eliminate physical limits.|So traffic rules no longer matter~Experience does not exempt a driver from rules.

PERSONAL|132|Imitation learning|What determines whether copying another driver's behaviour is useful?|Whether the behaviour being copied is safe and appropriate.|Imitation can teach good habits or reinforce dangerous ones.|Whether the driver has an expensive car~Car price does not prove good judgement.|Whether the driver is confident~Confidence can exist alongside unsafe habits.|Whether other people also do it~Common behaviour is not necessarily safe or lawful.

PERSONAL|132|Mature driving|Another driver stalls when the light turns green. What is the mature response?|Wait calmly and leave them room to recover.|Tolerance reduces pressure and helps prevent an ordinary mistake becoming a dangerous situation.|Sound the horn continuously~This adds stress rather than helping.|Drive very close to push them along~Tailgating increases danger.|Overtake without checking other traffic~Impatience does not justify an unsafe manoeuvre.

PERSONAL|133|Overconfidence|A new driver feels expert after a few months without an accident. What is the main concern?|They may underestimate risk and overestimate their ability.|Limited experience can produce confidence before reliable hazard judgement develops.|An accident-free period proves expert ability~It does not test every hazardous situation.|Confidence removes the need for safety margins~Margins are still necessary.|Only mechanical faults can now cause an accident~Human decisions remain a major risk.

PERSONAL|134|Probability learning|You rarely see trains at a crossing you use daily. What is the safe use of that experience?|Continue checking for trains every time.|A low past frequency does not make the next crossing safe.|Stop looking because trains are unlikely~Rare events can still occur.|Check only at the times you remember trains~Timetables and circumstances can change.|Use the car ahead as proof of safety~Conditions may change before you cross.

PERSONAL|134|Excessive stress|You are running late and feeling increasingly stressed. What is the best response?|Allow for the delay and continue driving calmly.|Excessive stress can narrow attention and impair judgement; speeding adds risk.|Take smaller gaps to regain time~That increases collision risk.|Use the horn to make others hurry~It does not make the journey safer.|Focus only on the destination~That draws attention away from current hazards.

PERSONAL|134|Planning time|How can you reduce stress before a journey?|Allow enough time and plan the route before setting off.|A realistic schedule reduces pressure to rush or make sudden decisions.|Plan to recover delays by speeding~That creates pressure and risk.|Leave route decisions until busy junctions~Last-second navigation increases distraction.|Choose the shortest following distance~This reduces safety margins rather than stress.

PERSONAL|135|Negative peer pressure|Passengers urge you to drive faster because they are late. What should you do?|Keep a safe lawful speed and explain that safety comes first.|The driver remains responsible even when passengers pressure them.|Speed up because passengers share responsibility~Pressure does not transfer the driver's duty.|Show your skill by taking bigger risks~That is precisely the dangerous response.|Let the loudest passenger choose your speed~Passengers do not control your legal obligations.

PERSONAL|135|Positive peer pressure|Which passenger behaviour can improve road safety?|Calmly asking the driver to slow down when driving unsafely.|Passengers can support safer choices rather than encourage risk-taking.|Distracting the driver during a difficult junction~This competes with essential attention.|Encouraging a risky overtake~That increases pressure to take risks.|Staying silent about dangerous driving~Silence can be interpreted as approval.

PERSONAL|140|Alcohol threshold|At what blood alcohol concentration does the numerical Swedish drink-driving limit begin?|0.2 per mille.|The numerical threshold is 0.2 per mille in blood, corresponding to 0.1 mg per litre of exhaled air.|0.2 percent~Percent and per mille differ by a factor of ten.|0.5 per mille~That is above Sweden's threshold.|1.0 per mille~That is the numerical threshold associated with aggravated drink-driving.

PERSONAL|140|Aggravated drink-driving threshold|Which blood alcohol level is the numerical threshold for aggravated drink-driving?|1.0 per mille.|A level of at least 1.0 per mille is one criterion for aggravated drink-driving; other circumstances can also matter.|0.1 per mille~That is not the aggravated numerical threshold.|0.2 per mille~That is the ordinary numerical drink-driving threshold.|2.0 per mille~Aggravated drink-driving can apply well below this level.

PERSONAL|141|Alcohol breakdown|What reliably speeds up the body's elimination of alcohol before driving?|None of these tricks; the body needs time.|Coffee, showers and exercise do not provide a reliable shortcut to alcohol elimination.|Drinking strong coffee~Feeling more alert does not remove alcohol faster.|Taking a cold shower~A shower does not accelerate the necessary metabolism.|Exercising hard for ten minutes~Exercise does not make you safely sober on demand.

PERSONAL|141|The morning after|You feel exhausted after drinking the previous evening. What should you consider before driving?|Both remaining alcohol and impaired fitness from fatigue.|Feeling hungover or sleep-deprived can impair driving even after alcohol levels decline.|Only whether you can smell alcohol~Smell cannot determine blood alcohol or fitness.|Coffee guarantees safe driving~Alertness does not establish sobriety or fitness.|Sleep always removes all alcohol overnight~The amount consumed and time elapsed matter.

PERSONAL|141|Prescribed medication|A prescribed medicine makes you drowsy. What should you do about driving?|Do not drive while impaired and seek advice about its effects.|A prescription does not authorise driving when the medicine makes you unsafe.|Drive because a doctor prescribed it~You remain responsible for safe driving.|Double the dose to finish treatment sooner~That can worsen impairment and is not driving advice.|Ignore the leaflet if the journey is short~A short journey can still involve serious hazards.

PERSONAL|142|Drugs and driving|What is a dangerous effect of stimulant drugs on driving?|Overconfidence while fatigue may be masked.|Feeling stimulated does not mean judgement and reaction are safe.|They guarantee better judgement~Stimulation can distort risk assessment.|They make sleep unnecessary~Suppressed tiredness does not remove the need for sleep.|They eliminate collision risk~No drug removes road hazards.

PERSONAL|143|Handheld phone|May you use a handheld phone while driving if you keep one hand on the wheel?|No.|The handheld-phone prohibition is not avoided by keeping the other hand on the wheel.|Yes if the call is short~Call duration does not create an exception.|Yes when using its speaker~Holding it while using speaker mode is still handheld use.|Yes on a familiar road~Familiarity does not remove distraction or the prohibition.

PERSONAL|143|Hands-free distraction|Why can a hands-free call still be dangerous?|The conversation can take attention away from driving.|Free hands do not guarantee an undistracted mind.|Hands-free calls cannot affect concentration~Conversation still uses mental attention.|Only the phone's weight creates risk~The cognitive distraction is important.|Hands-free makes road observation unnecessary~You must continue observing and responding to traffic.

PERSONAL|143|Navigation preparation|When should you enter a complicated destination into your navigation system?|Before moving off, or after stopping somewhere safe and permitted.|Navigation setup can divert eyes and attention from the road.|While entering a roundabout~A roundabout requires full attention.|While overtaking because the road is straight~Overtaking requires careful observation.|Whenever traffic behind is slow~Traffic speed does not remove distraction.

PERSONAL|148|Fatigue and legality|Can it be prohibited to drive because of tiredness?|Yes, if you cannot drive safely.|Fitness to drive includes fatigue, not just alcohol or illness.|No because tiredness cannot be measured like alcohol~The safety duty still applies.|No on a journey under ten kilometres~There is no general short-trip exemption.|Only professional drivers need to be rested~All drivers must be fit to drive.

PERSONAL|149|Fatigue warning signs|You yawn repeatedly and struggle to keep a steady speed. What should this prompt?|Stop safely and address the tiredness.|These are warning signs that concentration and control may be deteriorating.|Increase speed to arrive sooner~Higher speed increases consequences and workload.|Open a window and assume the problem is solved~Fresh air is not a reliable cure for fatigue.|Follow another vehicle very closely~That reduces reaction margin when you need more of it.

PERSONAL|150|Microsleep|What is microsleep in driving?|A brief unintended episode of sleep.|Even a very brief loss of awareness can cover a substantial distance at road speed.|A deliberate mirror check~Microsleep is a loss of wakefulness.|Normal blinking with full awareness~Microsleep involves sleep rather than ordinary blinking.|A safe way to rest on straight roads~Any sleep while driving is dangerous.

PERSONAL|150|Recovering from tiredness|What is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation?|Adequate sleep.|Temporary alertness measures do not replace restorative sleep.|Loud music~It cannot restore lost sleep.|Driving with the window open~Cool air may feel refreshing but is not a reliable remedy.|Concentrating harder indefinitely~Willpower does not prevent involuntary sleep.

PERSONAL|154|Central vision|Which task relies particularly on central vision?|Reading the precise wording on a road sign.|Central vision provides the detail needed to identify text and fine features.|Detecting only vague movement at the edge of sight~That is mainly a peripheral-vision function.|Hearing an approaching siren~That uses hearing rather than vision.|Feeling the car skid~That uses physical sensations as well as sight.

PERSONAL|154|Peripheral vision|Why is peripheral vision important in traffic?|It helps detect movement and potential hazards outside your direct focus.|You can then turn your eyes to inspect the detected hazard more precisely.|It reads small sign text better than central vision~Central vision is better for fine detail.|It is unaffected by alcohol and tiredness~Both can impair visual attention.|It eliminates the need to move your gaze~You still need active scanning.

PERSONAL|155|Scanning ahead|Which observation habit is generally safer?|Move your gaze and scan both near and far ahead.|Flexible scanning helps detect developing hazards before they become urgent.|Fix your gaze on the bumper ahead~That narrows your information to one small area.|Look only at road signs~Other road users and roadside activity matter too.|Watch the speedometer continuously~You must also watch the road and surrounding traffic.

PERSONAL|156|One headlight at night|You see one light approaching at night. What should you remember?|It may be a wider vehicle with a failed headlight.|Assuming every single light is a narrow motorcycle can lead to inadequate clearance.|It must be a bicycle~Several vehicle types can appear as one light.|It is safe to move towards the centre line~That reduces clearance if the vehicle is wider than expected.|Its speed must be low~The number of lights does not establish speed.

PERSONAL|157|Tunnel vision|What is a danger of tunnel vision?|Missing hazards at the sides of the road.|Stress, fatigue and alcohol can narrow attention to a smaller area.|Seeing too much roadside detail~Tunnel vision reduces peripheral awareness.|Automatically improving reaction time~Narrowed awareness may delay hazard detection.|Becoming immune to distractions~Tunnel vision is an impairment, not protection.

PERSONAL|93|Speed blindness|After a long motorway drive, 60 km/h feels unusually slow. What should you do?|Check the speedometer and adapt to the new road conditions.|Prolonged high speed can distort your subjective perception of speed.|Trust the feeling and accelerate~Your feeling may underestimate actual speed.|Keep motorway following distances only by intuition~Perception may be distorted.|Assume the speedometer is wrong~The changed feeling alone is not evidence of a fault.

ENVIRONMENT|304|Fossil carbon dioxide|Why does burning fossil petrol contribute to climate change?|It adds carbon dioxide from long-stored carbon to the atmosphere.|Carbon dioxide contributes to the enhanced greenhouse effect.|Because it removes all oxygen from the atmosphere~That is not the mechanism described.|Because carbon dioxide is the same gas as carbon monoxide~They are different compounds with different effects.|Because headlights heat the whole planet directly~Fuel-related greenhouse gas emissions are the relevant mechanism.

ENVIRONMENT|305|Catalytic converter warm-up|When is a conventional catalytic converter least effective?|Just after a cold engine is started.|It needs to reach operating temperature to treat exhaust effectively.|Only during summer~Cold-start temperature, not the season alone, is the issue.|Only after a long warm journey~A warmed converter normally works more effectively.|Whenever the headlights are on~Headlight use does not determine catalyst temperature.

ENVIRONMENT|305|Catalytic converter limits|Does a catalytic converter remove the climate impact of burning fossil fuel?|No, fossil carbon dioxide emissions remain.|Converters reduce several harmful pollutants but do not make fossil-fuel driving climate-neutral.|Yes, it removes all carbon dioxide~Conventional converters do not do that.|Yes, once the engine is warm~Warmth improves pollutant treatment, not elimination of fossil carbon.|Only at motorway speeds~Speed does not turn it into a carbon-capture device.

ENVIRONMENT|306|Engine-heater timer|Why use a timer with an engine heater?|To warm the engine when needed without wasting electricity.|Excessive heating time adds energy use without proportional benefit.|To run the heater continuously all year~That wastes electricity.|To avoid ever servicing the engine~Heating does not replace maintenance.|To warm the tyres instead of the engine~The device is intended to warm the engine.

ENVIRONMENT|306|Roof-box resistance|An empty roof box is no longer needed. What is the best choice for efficiency?|Remove it.|Even an empty roof box increases aerodynamic drag and can increase consumption.|Keep it because empty objects cause no drag~Air resistance does not depend only on weight.|Open its lid while driving~That increases drag and is unsafe.|Lower tyre pressure to compensate~Underinflation increases rolling resistance and harms handling.
